slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1940–1950 interpolation to November 1944, women 21+ outside the South, all enfranchised by the Nineteenth Amendment; turnout from the carried-forward women-to-men ratio, calibrated to each state's 1944 vote.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1940–1950 interpolation to November 1944, white adults (Mexican-origin adults counted as white, as in 1940) in the eleven former Confederate states, 18+ in Georgia, which lowered its voting age to 18 in 1943; calibrated to certified 1944 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1940–1950 interpolation to November 1944, Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states (18+ in Georgia); Smith v. Allwright struck down the white primary in April 1944, but poll taxes and literacy tests keep most disfranchised, so the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1944 comes out as it did: Roosevelt wins, 432–99. The closest state was Ohio, which went to Dewey by 0.4 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1940 and 1950 census counts interpolated to 1944 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1944 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: The President has done right by farmers through this depression and war. He's saying jobs for the boys when they come home, and that matters to us.
women.controlQuote: The President has done right by farmers through this depression and war. He's saying jobs for the boys when they come home, and that matters to us.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: The President has gotten us through so much these four years, and he promises jobs when our boys come home. That matters to me right now.
south-white.controlQuote: The President has gotten us through so much these four years, and he promises jobs when our boys come home. That matters to me right now.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: Been working steady these past years, better than the twenties ever were. The man in office now, he's seen us through the war, so I'll stick with him tomorrow.
